title: Publishing and Maintaining Actions
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of publishing and maintaining actions and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to publishing and maintaining actions.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on publishing and maintaining actions. Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Publishing and Maintaining Actions matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates. Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates. Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Repository setup for public actions
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Release versioning
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Tags and stable references
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Documentation and usage examples
items.text: Measure duration, resource/runner consumption, queue time, and failure rate before changing the pipeline. Bound retries, cancel stale work only when safe, and compare the result after one controlled change.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate tagged action release
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*.*.*"]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  validate-release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Validate version, tests, and release notes"
content_blocks.expected_output: A matching version tag triggers validation; the example intentionally does not publish anything or grant write permissions.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Test the tag filter in a sandbox and add release steps only after reviewing publication permissions.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Protect release tags and verify the selected ref is the expected source revision.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to publishing and maintaining actions. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain publishing and maintaining actions, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Package shared workflow logic behind clear input/output contracts and maintained versions.

content.task: Apply publishing and maintaining actions to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Publishing an action requires versioned releases, stable references, clear examples, compatibility notes, and a plan for deprecation and security updates.

Reuse the right abstraction: reusable workflows compose jobs; composite actions bundle steps; JavaScript or container actions package executable behavior. Define inputs, outputs, permissions, and versions explicitly.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
